title: DOM Events: Capture, Bubbling and Delegation
objectives: Trace an event through its capture, target and bubble phases
Use one delegated listener instead of one per element
Tell stopping propagation apart from cancelling the default action

cards.title: An event travels down the tree, then back up
cards.body: When you click a button inside a list inside the page, the browser builds a path from the window down to the button. The event first visits each ancestor going down (capture), then the button itself (target), then each ancestor again going up (bubble). A listener on any element on that path can react.

cards.title: Worked example: one listener for a 1,000-row table
cards.body: A table has 1,000 rows, each with Edit, Delete and Share buttons. One listener per button means 3,000 registrations, plus 3 more for every row added later. One listener on the table can read the event's target, find the nearest button and its row, and act. That is 1 registration, and new rows work with no extra code.

cards.title: The three phases of one click
cards.body: The path is fixed when dispatch starts, so moving nodes mid-event does not change it.
steps: Capture: window, document, html, body, table, tbody, row, cell (top down)
Target: the clicked button runs its own listeners
Bubble: cell, row, tbody, table, body, html, document, window (bottom up)
Default action: if nothing cancelled it, the browser does its normal behaviour, such as following a link

cards.title: Stop the journey or stop the default: two separate switches
cards.body: Stopping propagation ends the trip through ancestors, but the browser still follows the link or submits the form. Cancelling the default action stops the link or submission, but ancestors still hear the event. They are independent; code that needs both must ask for both.

cards.title: Trap: assuming every event bubbles
cards.body: focus, blur, mouseenter, mouseleave and a resource's load do not bubble, so a delegated listener on a parent never hears them in the bubble phase. Use the bubbling variants focusin and focusout, listen in the capture phase, or attach the listener directly to the element.

questions.prompt: A listener registered for the capture phase sits on a table, and the user clicks a button inside one of its rows. When does that listener run?

choices.label: Before the button's own listeners, on the way down
After the button's listeners, on the way back up
Only if the button's listener lets the event bubble
After the browser has run the click's default action

questions.explanation: Capture listeners run top down before the target phase; bubbling has not started yet, so stopping propagation at the button cannot prevent them.

questions.prompt: A chat list adds new message rows as they arrive, and each row has a Reply button. Which approach keeps working for rows added later with no extra code?

choices.label: Register a click listener on each Reply button once the page has loaded
One listener on the list that finds the closest Reply button to the event target
A capture-phase listener on each row, registered when the row is created
Re-register listeners on each button after the whole list re-renders

questions.explanation: The delegated listener lives on an element that already exists, so rows created later are covered by the bubble from their buttons.

questions.prompt: A link's click listener stops propagation but does not cancel the default action. What happens?

choices.label: Neither the parent listeners nor the navigation happen
Parent listeners run, but the browser does not navigate
Parent listeners do not run, but the browser still navigates
The browser asks the parent listeners whether to navigate

questions.explanation: Propagation and the default action are separate: stopping one does not stop the other.

questions.prompt: A form-wide listener on the form element wants to highlight whichever input gains focus. Which event should it listen for in the bubble phase?

choices.label: focus
focusin
change
mouseenter

questions.explanation: focus does not bubble, so a parent only hears it in the capture phase; focusin is the bubbling version. change fires on commit, not on focus.

questions.prompt: Order the listeners that run when a button inside a card is clicked. The card has a capture listener and a bubble listener; the button has one listener.

items.label: The card's bubble listener
The card's capture listener
The button's own listener

questions.explanation: Capture goes down to the target, the target runs, then the event bubbles back up through the card.

questions.prompt: A product grid shows 120 cards, each with 3 clickable controls. Per-element listeners need how many registrations, compared with 1 for delegation?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the count grows with every card loaded by infinite scroll, while the delegated listener stays at 1; delegation also removes the need to unregister listeners when cards are removed.

flashcards.back: Capture (top down), target, bubble (bottom up).
One listener on an ancestor; inspect the target to find which child was used.

flashcards.front: Stopping propagation vs cancelling the default action?
flashcards.back: One stops the trip through ancestors; the other cancels the browser's default action.

flashcards.front: Bubbling replacements for focus and blur?
flashcards.back: focusin and focusout.

sources.title: MDN: Event listener options (capture, once, passive)

mechanism.title: How the browser dispatches one event
steps: Something happens: a click, a key press, a network response. The browser creates an event object with a type, a target (the deepest element involved) and flags saying whether it bubbles and whether it can be cancelled.

Before any listener runs, the browser computes the propagation path: the target, then each parent up to the document and the window. The DOM Standard fixes this path at the start of dispatch, so removing an element from the tree during a listener does not change which ancestors the event visits.

Capture phase: listeners registered for capture run on each ancestor from the window downwards. This is how a container can see an event before its children do, for example to close a menu on any outside click.

Target phase: listeners on the target element run. Then, if the event type bubbles, the bubble phase runs listeners on each ancestor from the parent upwards. Most user-input events bubble; focus, blur, mouseenter, mouseleave and load on an element do not.

At any point a listener can stop propagation, which ends the trip after the current element (or immediately, for the immediate variant, which also skips other listeners on the same element). Separately, a listener can cancel the default action if the event is cancelable.

After dispatch, if no listener cancelled it, the browser performs the default action: following a link, submitting a form, inserting a typed character, scrolling. For touch and wheel events the browser cannot start scrolling until it knows whether some listener will cancel; a listener marked passive promises not to, so scrolling can start straight away.

useWhen: Use delegation for lists, tables and grids whose children are added and removed often.
Use a capture listener when a container must see an event before any child can stop it, such as outside-click detection or focus tracking.
avoidWhen: Avoid delegation for high-frequency events such as pointer moves over a large tree when only one small element cares; a listener on that element does less work per event.
Avoid stopping propagation to fix a local bug: it silently breaks analytics, outside-click handlers and delegated listeners higher up.

rows: No: each new element needs its own
Memory and setup time grow with the list; must unregister on removal
Each event must work out which child was used; fails for events that do not bubble
Runs before the target, so it can surprise code that expects to go first

numbers.title: Counting listeners on an infinite-scroll feed (illustrative)
assumptions: A feed loads 20 posts per page and the user scrolls through 50 pages
Each post has 4 controls: like, comment, share and a menu
steps: Posts loaded: 20 × 50 = 1,000.
Per-element listeners: 1,000 × 4 = 4,000 registrations, each one also an object the browser must keep.
If old posts are removed without unregistering their listeners and something still references them, those closures stay reachable.
Delegation: 1 listener on the feed container, whatever the number of posts.
numbers.result: Delegation turns a cost that grows with content into a constant, and removes a whole class of forgotten-cleanup bugs.

india.title: Edge case: passive listeners and scroll start
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: MDN's documentation of listener options explains that when a wheel or touch listener might cancel scrolling, the browser generally cannot start scrolling until that listener finishes, so a slow listener delays the scroll. Marking the listener passive promises it will not cancel, and the browser can scroll at once. To get this benefit in old code, the DOM specification makes passive the default for wheel, mousewheel, touchstart and touchmove listeners on the window, the document, the root element and the body, so cancelling scrolling there needs passive set to false explicitly.

pitfalls.trap: “I'll attach a click listener to each row as I render it.”
pitfalls.say: “I'd put one delegated listener on the table and find the row from the event target, so added rows work and nothing needs unregistering.”

pitfalls.trap: “Stopping propagation will stop the link from navigating.”
pitfalls.say: “That only stops ancestors hearing it; I'd cancel the default action to stop navigation.”

pitfalls.trap: “A delegated focus listener on the form will catch every field.”
pitfalls.say: “focus doesn't bubble; I'd use focusin or a capture-phase listener.”

takeaways: Events go down (capture), hit the target, then come back up (bubble).
One delegated listener on an ancestor handles any number of children, including future ones.
Stopping propagation and cancelling the default action are separate switches.
Check whether an event bubbles before delegating it; mark scroll-related listeners passive.

interactive.title: Who hears this click?
interactive.prompt: A modal has a backdrop with a click listener that closes the modal. Inside it, a Save button's listener stops propagation. The user clicks Save. Predict what happens.

choices.label: Save runs and the modal stays open
choices.feedback: Right: the event never bubbles from the button up to the backdrop's listener.

choices.label: Save runs, then the modal closes
choices.feedback: That would happen if propagation were not stopped, because the click bubbles to the backdrop.

choices.label: The modal closes before Save runs
choices.feedback: Only a capture-phase listener on the backdrop would run before the button.

interactive.reveal: Stopping propagation at the button ends the bubble phase there, so the backdrop's bubble listener never runs. A cleaner fix is to have the backdrop check whether the target is the backdrop itself, which keeps the event visible to analytics and other ancestors.

seeAlso.why: Listeners run as tasks on the event loop, so slow handlers delay rendering

title: Layout Systems: Normal Flow, Flexbox and Grid
objectives: Explain how normal flow places block and inline boxes
Choose between flexbox (one dimension) and grid (two dimensions)
Calculate how fr units share the free space

cards.title: Normal flow comes first
cards.body: Before any layout system is chosen, boxes follow normal flow. Block boxes stack vertically and take the full available width; inline boxes sit side by side on a line and wrap. Flexbox and grid are opted into on a container, and only that container's direct children become flex or grid items.

cards.title: Misconception: grid replaces flexbox
cards.body: Flexbox lays items out along one axis at a time and lets content size drive the result, which suits toolbars, tag lists and centring. Grid defines rows and columns together, so items line up in both directions, which suits page layouts and card galleries. Real pages mix both: a grid of cards, each card using flexbox inside.

cards.title: How a grid shares 1,000 px across 200px 1fr 2fr
cards.body: fr units divide only the space left after fixed tracks and gaps.
steps: Container: 1,000 px wide, columns 200px 1fr 2fr, gap 20 px
Fixed: 200 px track + 2 gaps × 20 px = 240 px
Free space: 1,000 − 240 = 760 px, shared over 3 fr
1fr ≈ 253.3 px and 2fr ≈ 506.7 px

cards.title: Content can still win against fr
cards.body: A plain 1fr track has a minimum of auto, so a long unbreakable word or a wide image can force its column wider than its share. Writing minmax(0, 1fr) lets the track shrink below its content, and the content then needs wrapping or overflow handling. The same idea applies to flex items, whose default minimum width is their content size.

cards.title: Trap: four 25% columns plus gaps
cards.body: Percentages are taken from the container's width, and gaps are added on top. Four 25% columns with three 16 px gaps need 100% + 48 px, so the grid overflows its container. fr units, or flex-grow, share the space after gaps instead.

questions.prompt: A page gallery must line cards up in both rows and columns as the window resizes. Which layout system is the natural fit?

choices.label: Flexbox with wrapping, sizing each card by its content
Grid, defining columns that every row shares
Normal flow, with every card set to an inline box
Absolute positioning, computing each card's offset

questions.explanation: Grid aligns items in two dimensions at once; wrapped flex lines are sized independently, so columns do not line up from row to row.

questions.prompt: A grid container is 900 px wide with columns 1fr 2fr and a 30 px gap. How wide is the 2fr column?

choices.label: 600 px
580 px
570 px
435 px

questions.explanation: Free space is 900 − 30 = 870 px over 3 fr, so 1fr is 290 px and 2fr is 580 px; 600 px forgets to subtract the gap.

questions.prompt: In a 1fr 1fr grid, one column holds a very long URL with no break points and grows wider than the other. What is the usual fix?

choices.label: Change both tracks to 50% widths
Use minmax(0, 1fr) and let the text wrap or scroll
Turn the grid into a wrapping flex row
Add a larger gap between the two tracks

questions.explanation: A plain 1fr has an automatic minimum equal to its content; minmax(0, 1fr) removes that floor so the tracks stay equal.

questions.prompt: Without any layout system set, how are two paragraphs placed inside a section?

choices.label: Side by side, wrapping onto a new line when full
Stacked vertically, each as wide as the section
Overlapping at the section's top-left corner
In equal columns sized to the widest paragraph

questions.explanation: Paragraphs are block boxes, so normal flow stacks them and stretches them to the available width; inline boxes are the ones that sit on a line.

questions.prompt: Order the steps a grid uses to size 200px 1fr 2fr columns in a fixed-width container.

items.label: Divide the remaining space by the total number of fr
Start from the container's width
Subtract the fixed track and the gaps
Give each fr track its multiple of one fr

questions.explanation: fr units only see the space that fixed tracks and gaps leave behind.

questions.prompt: A grid is 960 px wide with columns 1fr 1fr 2fr and two 16 px gaps. How wide is the 2fr column, in pixels?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 232 + 232 + 464 + 32 = 960, so the tracks and gaps fill the container to the pixel; forgetting the gaps gives 480 px and an overflow.

flashcards.front: Flexbox vs grid in one line?
flashcards.back: Flexbox: one axis, content-driven. Grid: rows and columns together.
The space left after fixed tracks and gaps.

flashcards.front: Why can a 1fr column grow past its share?
flashcards.back: Its minimum is auto (content size); use minmax(0, 1fr).

sources.title: MDN: Basic concepts of grid layout
W3C: CSS Grid Layout Module Level 1

mechanism.title: How the browser resolves a layout
steps: Layout starts at the root and works down. Each box asks its parent for an available width, works out its own width, lays out its children, and reports its height back up. That is why changing one element's size can move everything after it.

In normal flow, block boxes stack in the block direction (top to bottom in English) and fill the inline size of their container; inline content is broken into line boxes that wrap. Vertical margins between adjacent blocks can collapse into the larger of the two, a frequent source of surprise spacing.

A flex container lays its children along a main axis. Each item starts from its flex-basis (often its content size); if the line has spare space it is shared in proportion to flex-grow, and if it is short the deficit is taken in proportion to flex-shrink weighted by basis. With wrapping on, each line is sized independently, so items on different lines do not line up in columns.

A grid container first defines tracks. Fixed tracks (pixels, percentages) and gaps are taken out of the container's size; then fr tracks share what is left in proportion to their fr values, subject to each track's minimum. Items are then placed into cells by line numbers, names or auto-placement.

Track minimums matter. A plain 1fr behaves like minmax(auto, 1fr): it will not shrink below its content's minimum size. That protects content from being cut off but breaks equal columns when one cell holds wide content. minmax(0, 1fr) removes the floor.

Patterns such as repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)) let the grid decide how many columns fit, giving a responsive gallery without media queries; flexbox with flex-wrap gives a similar effect when columns need not align.

useWhen: Use grid when items must align in both rows and columns, such as a page shell or a card gallery.
Use flexbox for a row or column of items whose sizes come from their content, such as a toolbar, a button group or centring one item.
avoidWhen: Avoid percentage columns plus gaps when the total must fit; use fr or flex-grow so gaps come out first.
Avoid absolute positioning for whole layouts; positioned boxes leave normal flow, so siblings no longer make room and text resizing overlaps them.

rows: Content first, then grow and shrink
Toolbars, nav bars, centring, tag lists
Container first, tracks defined up front

numbers.title: Where 1,000 px goes in a 200px 1fr 2fr grid
assumptions: No content wider than its track
steps: Fixed space: the 200 px track plus two 20 px gaps, 240 px in all.
Free space for fr tracks: 1,000 − 240 = 760 px.
Columns: 200 px, ≈ 253.3 px and ≈ 506.7 px; plus 40 px of gaps = 1,000 px.
At 600 px wide, free space is 360 px and 1fr = 120 px; below that a single-column layout usually reads better.
numbers.result: fr tracks get only what fixed tracks and gaps leave, so narrowing the container shrinks the fr columns faster than the fixed one.

india.title: Edge case: the minimum size of an fr track
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The CSS Grid specification defines a flexible track sized with fr as having an automatic minimum unless the author sets one, (a bare 1fr means minmax(auto, 1fr)), so a common fix when columns must stay equal is minmax(0, 1fr). In practice a single long product code, URL or untranslated word in one cell can make a two-column layout lopsided on narrow screens. Testing layouts with long, unbreakable strings and large text sizes catches this before users do.

pitfalls.trap: “Use four 25% columns with a 16 px gap.”
pitfalls.say: “Percentages plus gaps overflow; I'd use repeat(4, 1fr) so the gaps are taken out first.”

pitfalls.trap: “Flexbox with wrap gives me a grid.”
pitfalls.say: “Each wrapped flex line sizes independently, so columns won't line up; I'd use grid when alignment across rows matters.”

takeaways: Normal flow stacks blocks and wraps inline content; layout systems are opted into per container.
Flexbox is one-dimensional and content-driven; grid is two-dimensional and container-driven.
fr shares the space left after fixed tracks and gaps.
A 1fr track will not shrink below its content unless you write minmax(0, 1fr).

interactive.title: Shrink the container
interactive.prompt: A grid uses columns 200px 1fr 2fr with two 20 px gaps. Slide the container width and watch how wide one fr becomes.
interactive.takeaway: At 1,000 px one fr is about 253.3 px. The 240 px of fixed track and gaps never shrinks, so at 560 px one fr is only about 106.7 px. That is the point to switch to a single column with a media query or an auto-fill grid.

seeAlso.why: Layout is the stage of the rendering pipeline these rules feed into

title: Responsive Design: Viewports, Breakpoints and Images
objectives: Explain CSS pixels, device pixels and the device pixel ratio
Use the viewport meta tag, media queries and container queries
Choose image sizes with srcset and sizes

cards.title: CSS pixels are not screen pixels
cards.body: Layout works in CSS pixels. A phone with a device pixel ratio (DPR) of 3 draws each CSS pixel with a 3 × 3 block of physical pixels. Without the viewport meta tag (width=device-width, initial-scale=1), mobile browsers lay the page out on a wide virtual viewport, often around 980 CSS px, and shrink it, so text becomes tiny.

cards.title: Worked example: the right image for a 360 px slot
cards.body: An image shows 360 CSS px wide on a DPR 3 phone, so it needs 360 × 3 = 1,080 device pixels across to look sharp. Sending a 2,160 px wide image doubles the width and quadruples the pixel count to download and decode. Sending 360 px looks blurry. srcset and sizes let the browser pick the closest file.

cards.title: How the browser picks from srcset
cards.body: The page lists files; the browser chooses, and may factor in network or data-saving preferences.
steps: srcset lists files with their real widths: 480w, 960w, 1440w
sizes says how wide the slot will be, for example 100vw on phones and 33vw on desktops
The browser multiplies the slot width by the DPR to get the pixels needed
It downloads one candidate close to that, before layout has finished

cards.title: Media queries ask about the page; container queries ask about the slot
cards.body: A media query changes styles based on the viewport, such as min-width: 48rem. A component reused in a sidebar and in a main column sees very different widths on the same screen, so a container query, which tests the size of the component's container, lets the card change layout where it actually sits.

cards.title: Trap: 100vh on mobile
cards.body: On many mobile browsers 100vh is the height with the address bar hidden, so a full-height hero with the bar showing pushes its button below the fold. The newer units svh (small), lvh (large) and dvh (dynamic) name which viewport you mean.

questions.prompt: A site has no viewport meta tag. On a phone, text looks tiny and the user must zoom. Why?

choices.label: The phone's DPR makes each CSS pixel physically smaller
The browser lays out on a wide virtual viewport and scales it down
The browser disables media queries when the tag is missing
The font files fail to load at small screen sizes

questions.explanation: Without width=device-width, mobile browsers assume a desktop-width layout viewport; DPR alone does not shrink CSS pixel sizes.

questions.prompt: An image fills a 400 CSS px slot on a DPR 2 laptop. Which candidate width is the best match?
questions.explanation: 400 CSS px × DPR 2 = 800 device pixels; 400w looks soft and 1,600w is four times the pixels needed.

questions.prompt: A product card appears in a narrow sidebar and in a wide main column on the same desktop page. Which tool lets the card change layout in each place?

choices.label: A media query on the viewport width
A container query on the card's container
A device pixel ratio media feature
A larger srcset with more candidates

questions.explanation: The viewport is the same for both cards; only the container differs, so a container query is the right test.

questions.prompt: A hero set to 100vh hides its call-to-action under the mobile address bar. Which unit fits the space visible while the bar is shown?

choices.label: 100lvh
100svh
100vw

questions.explanation: svh is the small viewport, measured with browser toolbars expanded; lvh is the large one, which matches the old 100vh behaviour on many browsers.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for choosing an image from srcset and sizes.

items.label: Read the slot width from sizes for the current viewport
Request the candidate closest to the pixels needed
Read the candidate files and widths listed in srcset
Multiply the slot width by the device pixel ratio

questions.explanation: The browser needs the candidates and the slot width before it can work out the pixels and pick a file.

questions.prompt: An image spans the full width of a 390 CSS px phone screen at DPR 3. How many device pixels wide should the ideal file be?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: a 1,170 px wide photo at the same aspect ratio has 9 times the pixels of a 390 px one, which is why serving one huge file to every device wastes so much on small screens.

flashcards.back: Device pixels per CSS pixel along one axis (2 or 3 on most phones).
width=device-width, initial-scale=1.
Small, large and dynamic viewport heights (toolbars shown, hidden, current).
Viewport size vs the size of the element's container.

sources.title: W3C: CSS Values and Units Module Level 4

mechanism.title: How a page adapts to the screen
steps: The layout viewport is the rectangle the page is laid out in. On desktop it is the window. On mobile, without a viewport meta tag, browsers pick a wide default so desktop sites do not break, then scale it down to fit. width=device-width makes the layout viewport as wide as the device in CSS pixels.

CSS pixels are a unit of layout, not hardware. The device pixel ratio says how many physical pixels draw one CSS pixel along each axis. Text and vector graphics are drawn crisply at any DPR; bitmap images need more pixels to stay sharp, which is why image choice depends on DPR.

Media queries apply styles when conditions on the viewport or device are true: width ranges, orientation, prefers-color-scheme, prefers-reduced-motion, hover capability. Breakpoints in rem units scale with the user's font size, so a user with larger text gets the narrower layout sooner.

Container queries apply styles based on the size of a declared container. This lets a component adapt to the space it actually has, which matters in design systems where the same card sits in sidebars, modals and full-width sections.

For images, srcset lists candidate files with their intrinsic widths and sizes tells the browser the slot width under each condition. The browser computes slot width × DPR and picks a candidate, possibly a smaller one on a constrained connection. The picture element is for art direction, through media conditions on its sources (such as a tighter crop on phones), and, through the type attribute, for offering newer formats with a fallback.

Viewport-percentage units (vw, vh) were defined before mobile toolbars appeared and disappeared during scroll. CSS Values Level 4 adds small, large and dynamic variants (svh, lvh, dvh and their width and inline equivalents). dvh tracks the current size but changes during scroll, which can cause layout jumps, so svh is often the safer choice for a hero.

useWhen: Use srcset with sizes for any content image whose display width varies with the screen.
Use container queries for reusable components that appear in slots of different widths.
avoidWhen: Avoid device-specific breakpoints such as one exact phone width; choose breakpoints where the content starts to look wrong.
Avoid dvh for large layout blocks that should not move while the user scrolls; svh or lvh is stable.

rows: Works at every width without breakpoints
Cannot reorganise content on its own
Blind to where a component sits
Slot width × DPR, plus browser hints
sizes must match the CSS or the pick is wrong

numbers.title: The cost of one oversized hero image (illustrative)
assumptions: Hero slot: 390 × 260 CSS px on a DPR 3 phone
The site sends one 3,000 × 2,000 px image to everyone
Decoded images use 4 bytes per pixel (RGBA)
steps: Pixels sent: 3,000 × 2,000 = 6,000,000, about 6.6 times more.
Decoded memory at 4 bytes per pixel: 24 MB for the 6,000,000 pixels sent, against about 3.7 MB for the 912,600 needed.
The download grows too, though compressed size does not scale exactly with pixel count.
numbers.result: Right-sizing with srcset cuts decode memory by roughly 6.6 times here and usually most of the download, which helps LCP on phones.

india.title: Why new viewport units were added
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The CSS Values and Units Level 4 specification defines the small, large and dynamic viewport sizes because mobile browsers show and hide toolbars as the user scrolls, so a single viewport height no longer describes what the user can see. MDN's viewport documentation also explains that without a viewport meta tag, mobile browsers render pages on a virtual viewport wider than the screen and then shrink the result. Both behaviours explain common mobile bugs: tiny text and hidden full-height buttons.

pitfalls.trap: “I'll export every image at 4,000 px so it looks sharp everywhere.”
pitfalls.say: “I'd generate a few widths and let srcset and sizes pick slot width × DPR.”

pitfalls.trap: “Breakpoints at 375 and 414 px, the iPhone widths.”
pitfalls.say: “I'd set breakpoints in rem where the content breaks, and let fluid layout handle widths in between.”

takeaways: Add width=device-width, initial-scale=1, or mobile pages render on a wide virtual viewport.
Image pixels needed = slot width in CSS px × DPR.
Media queries ask about the viewport; container queries ask about the component's space.
Use svh, lvh or dvh when mobile toolbars matter.

interactive.title: One card, two places
interactive.prompt: A product card is used in a 280 px sidebar and in a 900 px main column on the same desktop page. Below 400 px of its own width it should stack its image above the text.

choices.label: A container query on the card's wrapper at 400 px
choices.feedback: Right: the card reacts to its own available width wherever it is placed.

choices.label: A media query at a viewport width of 400 px
choices.feedback: On a desktop the viewport is usually far wider than 400 px, so the narrow sidebar card would not stack.

choices.label: A separate sidebar-card component with its own styles
choices.feedback: It works, but now two components must be kept in sync.

interactive.reveal: When the same component appears in containers of different widths on one screen, only a container query sees the difference. Media queries remain the tool for page-level layout and user preferences such as reduced motion.

seeAlso.why: Oversized hero images are a common cause of slow Largest Contentful Paint

title: Real-Time on the Client: Polling, SSE and WebSockets
objectives: Compare short polling, long polling, server-sent events and WebSockets
Explain the WebSocket upgrade handshake and SSE reconnection
Design reconnects that do not overload the server

cards.title: Four ways to hear about new data
cards.body: Short polling asks the server on a timer, whether or not anything changed. Long polling asks and the server holds the request open until there is news. Server-sent events (SSE) keep one HTTP response open and stream text events from server to browser. A WebSocket upgrades one connection into a two-way channel for messages in both directions.

cards.title: Worked example: seven tabs over HTTP/1.1
cards.body: Browsers open at most about six connections per host over HTTP/1.1, and each SSE stream holds one open for as long as the page lives.
steps: A user opens the same dashboard in seven tabs; each tab opens its own SSE stream
Six streams take all six connections to that host
The seventh stream, and every fetch the pages make to that host, waits for a free connection
Over HTTP/2 all streams share one connection (the server negotiates how many, often 100), so the limit disappears
Alternatives: one shared stream for all tabs of the site, or serve the stream over HTTP/2

cards.title: Opening a WebSocket
cards.body: It starts as ordinary HTTP, so it passes through the same ports, TLS and many proxies.
steps: Browser sends an HTTP GET with Upgrade: websocket and a random Sec-WebSocket-Key
Server answers 101 Switching Protocols with a Sec-WebSocket-Accept derived from that key
Both sides now exchange framed messages, text or binary, in either direction
Ping and pong frames check the link; a close frame ends it cleanly

cards.title: SSE reconnects for you, WebSockets do not
cards.body: The browser's SSE client reconnects on its own after a dropped stream, waiting a delay the server can set with a retry field, and sends the last event id it saw in a Last-Event-ID header so the server can resume. A WebSocket that drops just closes; the page must notice, reconnect and ask for anything it missed.

cards.title: Trap: reconnecting in lockstep
cards.body: When a server restarts, every client loses its connection at the same moment. If each one retries after a fixed 1 s, they all arrive together and can knock the server over again. Use exponential backoff with random jitter so reconnects spread out.

questions.prompt: An SSE stream drops and the browser reconnects on its own. What does it send so the server can resume?

choices.label: A Last-Event-ID header with the last id it saw
The full list of events it has already received
A WebSocket upgrade request for the same URL
A new random session token in the query string

questions.explanation: The browser remembers the last event id and sends it on reconnect; the server replays what came after it.

questions.prompt: What status code does a server send to accept a WebSocket upgrade?

choices.label: 200 OK
101 Switching Protocols
204 No Content
426 Upgrade Required

questions.explanation: RFC 6455 completes the handshake with 101; 426 is what a server sends when it requires the client to upgrade.

questions.prompt: A collaborative whiteboard sends many small binary updates from each user and receives everyone else's. Which transport suits it?

choices.label: Server-sent events, one stream per user
Short polling every 200 ms for changes
A WebSocket per open board
Long polling with batched uploads

questions.explanation: Frequent messages in both directions, including binary, are what WebSockets are for; SSE is server-to-client text only.

questions.prompt: A chat server restarts and 50,000 clients drop at once. Which reconnect policy is safest?

choices.label: Retry after a fixed 1 s delay
Retry at once, then each second
Exponential backoff with random jitter
Retry when the user next types

questions.explanation: Jitter spreads the reconnects over time, and backoff slows retries further if the server is still struggling.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of opening and using a WebSocket.

items.label: Both sides exchange framed messages
The client sends an HTTP GET with Upgrade: websocket
One side sends a close frame
The server replies 101 Switching Protocols

questions.explanation: Every WebSocket begins as an HTTP request, and only after the 101 reply do frames flow.

questions.prompt: After a server restart, 50,000 clients reconnect, each after a random delay spread evenly over 0–20 seconds. About how many reconnects per second reach the server?
questions.explanation: Design implication: without jitter all 50,000 arrive in the same second; spreading over 20 s cuts the peak 20 times.

flashcards.back: SSE: server to client, text. WebSocket: both ways, text or binary.
101 Switching Protocols with Sec-WebSocket-Accept.
Auto-reconnect, sending Last-Event-ID.
Exponential backoff with random jitter.

mechanism.title: How each technique keeps the page current
steps: Short polling: the page sends a normal request every N seconds. It is simple and works through any proxy, but most responses are empty when data changes rarely, and updates arrive up to N seconds late.

Long polling: the page sends a request and the server keeps it open until there is something to say or a timeout passes, then the page sends the next one. Latency is low, but each message costs a full request and response, and the server must hold one pending request per client.

Server-sent events: the page opens one GET and the server replies with Content-Type text/event-stream, writing events as lines of text (data, event, id and retry fields) and never finishing the response. The browser parses each event as it arrives. If the stream drops, the browser waits the retry delay, reconnects and sends Last-Event-ID so the server can replay anything missed.

WebSockets: the page sends an HTTP/1.1 GET with Upgrade: websocket and a random key; the server proves it understood by replying 101 Switching Protocols with a hash of that key. From then on the TCP connection carries frames, not HTTP: text or binary data frames and control frames (ping, pong, close). Frames from browser to server are masked, which RFC 6455 requires to protect intermediaries that might misread the traffic.

Neither SSE nor WebSockets solves missed messages across a full disconnect on its own. A robust client keeps a cursor (an event id or sequence number), reconnects with backoff and jitter, and asks the server for everything after that cursor, falling back to a full refetch if the gap is too old.

On the server side, long-lived connections change capacity planning: the limit becomes open connections and memory per connection rather than requests per second, and load balancers need idle timeouts longer than the heartbeat interval.

useWhen: Use SSE for one-way feeds such as notifications, live scores, progress updates and token-by-token text output.
Use WebSockets when the client also sends frequent messages, or messages are binary: chat, games, collaborative editing.
avoidWhen: Avoid any persistent connection when data changes every few minutes and a short delay is fine; polling with HTTP caching is simpler.
Avoid SSE over HTTP/1.1 with many tabs open to one site; browsers cap connections per domain, as MDN warns.

rows: One full request per message; held requests
One open connection per client; text only
Open connections; reconnect and resume are up to you

numbers.title: Polling cost against update rate (illustrative)
assumptions: 20,000 users keep an order-status page open
Each order changes status about once every 2 minutes
Option A polls every 4 s; option B uses SSE
steps: Polling load: 20,000 ÷ 4 = 5,000 requests/s.
Useful updates: 20,000 ÷ 120 s ≈ 167 per second.
So about 167 ÷ 5,000 ≈ 3.3% of polls return news; the rest are empty.
With SSE: about 167 small messages per second over 20,000 open connections, plus periodic heartbeats.
numbers.result: When updates are rare compared with the polling rate, pushing removes most requests, at the cost of holding connections open.

india.title: Edge case: the per-domain connection limit for SSE
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: MDN's EventSource documentation warns that when SSE is used over HTTP/1.1 rather than HTTP/2, it is subject to the browser's limit on open connections per domain, which is low (six in common browsers). Each tab with an open stream uses one, so a user with several tabs open to the same site can find that new requests to that domain stall. Over HTTP/2, streams share one connection and the limit is much higher, so serve SSE over HTTP/2 or share one stream across tabs.

pitfalls.say: “Notifications are one-way text, so I'd use SSE and get reconnection and resume from the browser for free.”

pitfalls.trap: “If the socket drops, reconnect every second.”
pitfalls.say: “I'd reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter, then fetch everything after the last sequence number I saw.”

takeaways: Polling pays per request whether or not anything changed; push pays per open connection.
SSE: one-way text over HTTP with built-in reconnect and Last-Event-ID resume.
WebSocket: HTTP upgrade (101), then two-way frames; reconnect and resume are your job.
Reconnect with backoff and jitter, and resume from a cursor.

interactive.title: What happens to the seventh tab?
interactive.prompt: A user opens the same dashboard in seven tabs. Each tab opens its own server-sent events stream to the site over HTTP/1.1, and the pages also fetch data from the same host.

choices.label: The seventh stream and later fetches wait for a free connection
choices.feedback: Right: six long-lived streams use all six connections the browser allows per host over HTTP/1.1.

choices.label: All seven streams share one connection automatically
choices.feedback: That is how HTTP/2 behaves, not HTTP/1.1.

choices.label: The server rejects the seventh stream with 429
choices.feedback: The request never reaches the server; it waits in the browser.

interactive.reveal: Share one stream across tabs, or serve the site over HTTP/2, where streams share one connection.

seeAlso.why: The system design view of pushing live updates through gateways and pub/sub

title: Memory Leaks in Long-Lived Pages
objectives: Explain garbage collection as reachability from roots
Recognise the common leak patterns in single-page apps
Find a leak with heap snapshots

cards.title: Garbage collection follows references
cards.body: The browser's garbage collector frees an object when nothing reachable from a root (the global object, the current call stack, live DOM) refers to it any more. A leak in a web page is not lost memory but forgotten memory: something reachable still points at data you no longer need.

cards.title: Misconception: removing an element frees it
cards.body: Removing a node from the document takes it out of the page, but if a variable, a cache or a closure still references it, the node and its whole subtree stay in memory. DevTools shows these as detached elements. Removal frees memory only when the last reference goes.

cards.title: Five references that keep old screens alive
cards.body: Each one is a path from a root to data from a screen the user has left.
steps: Listeners on window or document that are never unregistered
Timers and intervals still running for an unmounted view
Subscriptions to a store, socket or event bus never cancelled
Module-level caches and maps that only grow
Detached DOM nodes referenced from any of the above

cards.title: Finding a leak: repeat, snapshot, compare
cards.body: Take a heap snapshot, repeat one action several times (open and close a dialog, navigate away and back), force garbage collection and take another. Objects whose count grows with each repetition are the leak. The retainers view shows which reference chain keeps them alive.

cards.title: Trap: caching by element in a plain map
cards.body: A map from element to computed data holds every element strongly, so removed elements can never be collected. A weak-keyed map holds its keys weakly: when the element is otherwise unreachable, the entry goes with it. Choose the weak version for metadata attached to objects you do not own.

questions.prompt: When can the garbage collector free an object?

choices.label: When the page has not used it for a few minutes
When no chain of references from a root reaches it
When its element is removed from the document
When the tab moves to the background

questions.explanation: Modern collectors use reachability (mark-and-sweep); time since last use and removal from the page do not matter while a reference remains.

questions.prompt: After closing a modal 20 times, a heap snapshot shows 20 copies of the modal's elements marked detached. What is the most likely cause?

choices.label: The browser keeps closed modals for the back button
Something still references each closed modal's elements
Detached elements are freed only on page reload
The modal's CSS animations keep each copy alive

questions.explanation: Detached elements survive only while referenced; one copy per close means each open leaves a reference behind, often a listener or a cache entry.

questions.prompt: A dashboard view starts a 1-second refresh timer when it opens. Users switch views all day and memory climbs. What fix targets the cause?

choices.label: Lower the refresh rate to once every 10 seconds
Clear the timer when the view is closed
Reload the page every hour in the background
Move the refresh work into a web worker

questions.explanation: The timer's callback keeps the closed view's data reachable and keeps running; slowing it or moving it only changes how fast the leak grows.

questions.prompt: A library attaches computed metadata to elements it does not create, and those elements may be removed at any time. What should it store the metadata in?

choices.label: A plain map keyed by element
A weak-keyed map keyed by element
A global array of pairs
Session storage, by element id

questions.explanation: A weak-keyed map does not keep its keys alive, so entries disappear with their elements; the plain map and array keep every element forever.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for confirming a suspected leak with heap snapshots.

items.label: Repeat the suspect action several times
Load the page
Force garbage collection, take a snapshot and compare
Take a baseline snapshot
Do the action once to warm up caches

questions.explanation: Warm up before the baseline so one-time caches are not counted as growth, then compare after repeats and a forced collection.

questions.prompt: Each route change leaks 2.5 MB. A field agent's tab starts at 60 MB and they change route 80 times in a shift. How large is the heap at the end, in MB?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: a leak that is invisible in a 5-minute test (a few MB) becomes hundreds of MB over a working day, so test long sessions, not just page loads.

flashcards.back: No reference chain from a root reaches it.
Removed from the document but still referenced, so still in memory.
Global listeners, timers, subscriptions, growing caches.

flashcards.front: Plain map vs weak-keyed map for element metadata?
flashcards.back: The weak-keyed map: it does not keep the element alive.

sources.title: Chrome for Developers: Fix memory problems

mechanism.title: How memory is kept and released in a page
steps: Every object, closure, DOM node and buffer lives on the heap. The garbage collector periodically marks everything reachable from the roots (globals, the active call stack, the live document, pending callbacks) and frees the rest. MDN describes this mark-and-sweep approach; it handles cycles, so two objects pointing at each other are freed together once nothing else reaches them.

Closures capture the variables of the scope they were created in. A small listener function can therefore keep a large array, a component's whole state or a set of DOM nodes alive for as long as the listener itself is reachable.

Registered listeners, timers, animation-frame callbacks, observers and open sockets are all reachable from roots by design: the browser must be able to call them. Anything they capture stays alive until they are unregistered, cleared, disconnected or closed.

Single-page apps make this worse because the page never reloads. On a traditional site, navigation throws the whole heap away. In an app that swaps views, each view must undo what it set up, or every visit adds another copy of its state.

Weak references help when you attach data to objects whose lifetime you do not control. Weak-keyed maps and weak sets do not keep their keys alive. Weak references and finalisation callbacks exist too, but their timing is up to the collector, so they suit caches, not program logic.

Detection is empirical. In the browser's memory tools, compare heap snapshots taken before and after repeating an action, or record allocations over time. Look for object counts that grow with the number of repetitions, then read the retainer chain to find the root that holds them.

useWhen: Profile memory for apps that stay open for hours: dashboards, email, chat, support consoles and editors.
Pair every setup with a teardown: register and unregister, start and clear, subscribe and unsubscribe.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating a high but stable heap as a leak; caches and pooled objects can be deliberate. Growth per repetition is the signal.
Avoid weak-reference logic that must run at a known time; the collector decides when, and may never collect in a short session.

rows: Bounded caches with an eviction rule
Values while the key is alive
Metadata on elements or objects you do not own
Data that is expensive to recompute

numbers.title: How a small leak grows over a working day (illustrative)
assumptions: Each route change leaves 3 MB reachable (a view's state plus its detached DOM)
An agent changes route about 25 times an hour for 8 hours
Budget: 150 MB before the agent’s low-memory tablet starts discarding tabs
steps: Route changes in a day: 25 × 8 = 200.
Leaked memory: 200 × 3 MB = 600 MB.
Heap at end of day: 40 + 600 = 640 MB.
The budget is crossed after (150 − 40) ÷ 3 ≈ 37 route changes, about an hour and a half into the shift.
numbers.result: A 3 MB leak passes a quick test but breaks the app within the first two hours of real use.

india.title: Edge case: detached elements in the memory tools
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Chrome's DevTools documentation on fixing memory problems describes detached DOM trees: nodes removed from the document that are still referenced by script and so cannot be collected. It recommends heap snapshots, searching them for detached nodes, and reading the retainers to find which variable or listener holds them. It also suggests recording allocations on a timeline while repeating an action, because memory that climbs with each repetition and does not fall back after collection is the sign of a leak.

pitfalls.trap: “Memory is high, so we have a leak.”
pitfalls.say: “I'd check whether it grows with each repetition of an action; a high but flat heap may just be caching.”

pitfalls.trap: “We remove the elements when the view closes, so it's fine.”
pitfalls.say: “Removal frees nothing while a listener, timer or cache still references them; I'd tear those down too.”

takeaways: The collector frees what is unreachable, so a leak is an unwanted reference.
Global listeners, timers, subscriptions and growing caches are the usual culprits.
Every setup needs a matching teardown when a view closes.
Find leaks by repeating an action and comparing heap snapshots.

interactive.title: Watch a 3 MB leak add up
interactive.prompt: A page starts at 40 MB and each route change leaks 3 MB. Slide the number of route changes and see when the heap passes a 150 MB budget.
interactive.takeaway: At 20 route changes the heap is 100 MB and looks fine. By 40 it is 160 MB and over budget, and at 100 it reaches 340 MB. Short tests miss leaks; long sessions find them.

seeAlso.why: Client-side caches and subscriptions are where many app leaks start

title: Smooth Animation: Compositing and Layers
objectives: Say which CSS properties trigger layout, paint or only compositing
Explain what will-change does and what layers cost
Avoid forced synchronous layout in animation code

cards.title: Each frame redoes only the stages you dirty
cards.body: Animating width, height, top or left changes geometry, so every frame reruns layout, paint and compositing. Animating colour or a shadow skips layout but still repaints. Animating transform or opacity on an element with its own layer can skip both and only recomposite, which the browser can often do off the main thread.

cards.title: Worked example: promote only while animating
cards.body: A grid has 400 cards of 300 × 200 CSS px on a DPR 2 laptop, and any card can lift on hover.
steps: Promoting every card in advance: each layer is up to (600 × 400) device px × 4 B ≈ 0.96 MB, so about 384 MB for 400 cards
Instead, add will-change: transform to a card only when the pointer enters it
Animate transform on that one card
Remove the hint when the animation ends
At most a few layers exist at once: a few MB instead of hundreds

cards.title: Which stage each property reaches
cards.body: Cheaper animations stop earlier in the pipeline.
steps: Layout, paint and composite: width, height, top, left, margin, font-size
Paint and composite: color, background-color, box-shadow, border-radius
Composite only, on its own layer: transform, opacity
Some filters can be composited too, depending on the browser

cards.title: Layers are memory, not magic
cards.body: will-change: transform hints that an element will animate, so the browser may give it a compositor layer in advance. Each layer is a bitmap: a 1,000 × 800 px layer at 4 bytes per pixel is about 3.2 MB, and DPR 2 quadruples that. Promote what is about to animate, and remove the hint afterwards.

cards.title: Trap: forced layout inside an animation loop
cards.body: Reading a size or position right after changing styles forces layout immediately, and doing it per element is layout thrashing (covered in How Browsers Render a Page). In animation code, read every measurement first, then make every write.

questions.prompt: A 1,000 × 800 CSS px panel gets its own layer on a DPR 2 laptop. At 4 bytes per pixel, about how much memory can that layer take?

choices.label: 3.2 MB
6.4 MB

questions.explanation: (1,000 × 2) × (800 × 2) × 4 B = 12.8 MB: DPR 2 quadruples the 3.2 MB of a DPR 1 layer.

questions.prompt: A developer adds will-change: transform to all 400 cards in a grid to make hover effects smooth. What is the main risk?

choices.label: Hover effects stop running on the compositor
Each card may get its own layer, using a lot of memory
The cards lose their position in the grid layout
The browser ignores the hint on more than ten elements

questions.explanation: Layers are bitmaps; hundreds of them can exhaust graphics memory and slow compositing. MDN describes will-change as a last resort for known performance problems.

questions.prompt: A spinner is rotated by a script that sets its transform on every animation frame. The main thread then runs a 300 ms task. What happens to the spinner?

choices.label: It keeps turning on the compositor thread
It freezes until the task finishes
It speeds up later to catch up
It switches to a CSS animation

questions.explanation: Script-driven frames need the main thread; only animations handed to the compositor keep running while it is busy.

questions.prompt: A fade-in animates opacity from 0 to 1 on a card. Which stages does it need on each frame once the card has its own layer?

choices.label: Layout, paint and composite
Paint and composite
Composite only
Style and layout only

questions.explanation: Opacity is applied when layers are combined, so the compositor can blend the existing bitmap without repainting it.

questions.prompt: Order these animated properties from cheapest to most expensive per frame.

items.label: width
opacity
background-color

questions.explanation: opacity only composites, background-color repaints, and width relays out, repaints and composites.

questions.prompt: A full-screen layer is 1,920 × 1,080 CSS px on a DPR 1 screen at 4 bytes per pixel. About how many MB does it use?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: at DPR 2 the same layer has four times the pixels, about 33 MB, so a handful of promoted full-screen layers can use hundreds of MB on a high-density screen.

flashcards.back: transform and opacity.
Hints the element will change so the browser can prepare, often by creating a layer.
Width × height × DPR² × 4 bytes.
Interleaved style writes and size reads forcing repeated layouts; batch reads, then writes.

sources.title: web.dev: Stick to compositor-only properties and manage layer count
web.dev: How to create high-performance CSS animations

mechanism.title: What happens on each frame of an animation
steps: On every frame the browser may run script, recalculate styles, run layout, paint and composite. Which of these it must redo depends on what changed. A change to geometry dirties layout, and layout dirties paint for whatever moved. A change to colour dirties paint only. A change to transform or opacity on a layer dirties only compositing.

Painting records drawing commands and rasterises them into bitmaps. Compositing takes those bitmaps, the layers, and combines them with each layer's transform and opacity to make the final frame, usually on the GPU and on a separate compositor thread.

Because the compositor thread does not wait for the main thread, a transform or opacity animation that has been handed to it can stay smooth even while script is busy. A left or width animation cannot, because layout runs on the main thread.

Elements get their own layers for several reasons: 3D transforms, video, canvas, an animation of transform or opacity in progress, or will-change. A layer avoids repainting its neighbours when it moves, but costs memory proportional to its pixel area and adds work to compositing. Too many layers can be slower than none.

Forced synchronous layout happens when code changes styles and then reads a geometric value such as an element's size, position or scroll offset in the same frame. The browser must lay out immediately to return a correct value. Doing this per element in a loop multiplies layout cost; batching all reads before all writes, or deferring writes to the next frame callback, avoids it.
Animations should respect the prefers-reduced-motion media feature: for users who ask for less motion, replace movement with a quick fade or no animation.

useWhen: Use transform and opacity for movement, scaling, fades and slide-ins.
Use will-change briefly on an element just before a known, expensive animation, and remove it afterwards.
avoidWhen: Avoid animating width, height, top, left or margin on large or complex pages; animate transform: scale or translate instead where the design allows.
Avoid blanket will-change rules in stylesheets; MDN describes it as a last resort for existing performance problems.

columns: Can run off the main thread
rows: Cost grows with painted area; large blurs are slow
Needs a layer; layers cost memory

numbers.title: The memory bill for promoted layers (illustrative, upper bound)
assumptions: A page promotes 12 cards with will-change: transform
4 bytes per pixel; browsers may rasterise only tiles near the viewport, so this is an upper bound
steps: Memory per card layer: 777,600 × 4 B = 3,110,400 B ≈ 3.1 MB.
Twelve cards: 12 × 3.1 MB ≈ 37 MB of layer memory before anything moves.
Promoting only the card being animated keeps it near 3 MB.
numbers.result: Layer memory scales with area × DPR²; promote only what is about to animate.

india.title: What the performance guides recommend
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: web.dev's guide to compositor-only properties recommends animating only transform and opacity where possible, because changes to them can be handled by compositing without layout or paint, and warns that promoting too many elements to layers costs memory and management time and can make performance worse. MDN's will-change page goes further: it calls the property a last resort for existing performance problems, says not to apply it to many elements, and suggests setting it from script shortly before a change and removing it afterwards.

pitfalls.trap: “Add will-change to everything that might animate.”
pitfalls.say: “Each layer costs memory, about width × height × DPR² × 4 bytes; I'd set it just before an animation and remove it after.”
“That relays out every frame; I'd animate transform: translateX so it only recomposites.”

takeaways: Geometry changes cost layout, paint and composite; colour changes cost paint; transform and opacity only composite.
Compositor animations can stay smooth while the main thread is busy.
Layers cost about width × height × DPR² × 4 bytes each, so promote sparingly.
Batch size reads before style writes to avoid layout thrashing.

interactive.title: Which animation stutters?
interactive.prompt: A page runs a 300 ms search filter on the main thread while two loading spinners rotate. Spinner A is a CSS animation of transform: rotate; spinner B is a CSS animation of left and top that moves it around a small circle. Predict which keeps moving smoothly.

choices.label: Spinner A
choices.feedback: Right: a transform animation on its own layer can be driven by the compositor thread while script runs.

choices.label: Spinner B
choices.feedback: Margin changes need layout on the main thread, which is busy with the filter for 300 ms.

choices.label: Both freeze for 300 ms
choices.feedback: Only animations that need the main thread wait; compositor animations do not.

interactive.reveal: Main-thread work blocks layout and paint, so animations that need them freeze. Transform and opacity animations handed to the compositor keep running, which is why they are the default choice for motion.

seeAlso.why: The full rendering pipeline that these animation costs come from
